justification: run-code is green 3/3 consecutive runs, identical every time (blocks=30, executed=15, no flakiness) — every non-wildcarded expected-output block (reverse-space 80,024/0; counts-solved 1,048 flat at n=1,000/10,000/100,000; sort-space quicksort 0 B at every n vs merge sort's exact linear bytes; quicksort-depth 26 random / 4,999 sorted at n=5,000; bug-solved shared-vs-per-call exact byte tables; struct-class-array 1,600,024/4,000,024; stackalloc-sum 280/0; threshold-solved 0/40,024; fib-tradeoff heap bytes 0/2,000/0 across n=20..38) is checked for an exact string match by tools/run-code.mjs and passed identically on all three runs, which is itself strong evidence these deterministic byte counts are stable on this machine. I re-derived the arithmetic behind every one by hand: 10,000x8+24=80,024; 256x4+24=1,048; 100,000x16+24=1,600,024 and 100,000x8+24 + 100,000x32=4,000,024 (32 = 16-byte .NET object header + 16 bytes of two doubles, no further padding needed); 64x4+24=280; 10,000x4+24=40,024; merge sort's per-call-buffer bytes at n=1,000/2,000/4,000/8,000 match a geometric series consistent with Theta(n log n) extra allocation from the deliberately buggy version. I ran the RecursiveSum/InsufficientExecutionStackException stack-frame-differencing program myself, standalone, independent of the article's own code, at four stack sizes (1/2/4/8 MiB) across three full repeats: the differenced per-frame estimate came out to 63.97-64.06 B/frame on every pairing regardless of which two stack sizes were compared, while the raw depth for a fixed stack size wobbled by a few dozen frames run to run exactly as the article says. This is a real, independently reproduced confirmation that EnsureSufficientExecutionStack's undocumented safety margin behaves as a constant across stack sizes and genuinely cancels out of the subtraction -- not a plausible-sounding trick but a technique that measurably works, and a legitimately original contribution for an introductory CS page. I reproduced the stackalloc-widened-frame exercise the same way and got 3,363-3,367 frames at 1 MiB and 14,927-14,931 at 4 MiB across three runs, landing on the article's own ~272 B/frame every time -- the illustrative 'One run printed' numbers in the article (not covered by run-code.mjs's exact-match check, since they sit in plain ```text blocks rather than a checked ```text output block) are real and reproducible, not invented. I also reproduced the Dictionary<int,long> byte-flatness claim standalone across n=20..75 and confirmed the resize boundary sits between 38 and 50, so 'a dictionary sized for ~20 entries already has room for ~38' is factually correct, not just a plausible-sounding gloss on a coincidence. All eight cited primary sources were fetched directly: every quoted phrase (GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread's 'bytes allocated on the managed heap'; EnsureSufficientExecutionStack's 'an artificially limited stack that preserves enough space for an exception to be raised and recovery action to be taken' and 'is useful in situations where stack overflow might occur as a result of unbounded recursion'; StackOverflowException's 'you can't catch a StackOverflowException object with a try/catch block, and the corresponding process is terminated by default'; the Thread(..., maxStackSize) 'the maximum stack size, in bytes, to be used by the thread'; Span<T>'s ref-struct restriction list verbatim; stackalloc's 'automatically discarded when that method returns', 'the amount of memory available on the stack is limited...a StackOverflowException is thrown', and 'terminates the process as quickly as possible'; and Sedgewick & Wayne's 16-byte object overhead / 8-byte padding / 24-byte array header quotes and quicksort's 'it is in-place (uses only a small auxiliary stack)') matched the live pages verbatim or within a word. The cross-reference to Value Types vs Reference Types is accurate and present in this worktree: that article's own measured figure is 'a ClassTank costs 24 bytes, of which 4 are the int and the rest is the per-object overhead and padding,' which is exactly the 24-bytes-all-overhead-for-4-bytes-of-data figure this article cites, and both anchors linked (#are-structs-on-the-stack-measure-it, #when-a-struct-is-the-right-call) are real headings in that file. The Big-O Notation cross-reference is also accurate: its MergeSort allocates one n-sized buffer at the top and threads it through Split, exactly the pattern this article says it reuses, and #when-the-dropped-constant-decides-the-winner is a real heading there. Quicksort's depth numbers check out by hand too: log2(5,000)=12.3, and a Lomuto-style partition with the last element as pivot on an ascending array puts every element on one side, giving exactly n-1=4,999 levels; 26 for random input against a ~12.3 balanced-case lower bound is the expected ~2x constant for un-tail-call-optimized randomized quicksort recursion depth. Framing checks out too: naive Fibonacci's real cost being invisible to the heap counter is not rhetorical convenience -- GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread's own docs say nothing about the stack and count only managed-heap bytes, which I confirmed by reading the live page. Against comparable public treatments of space complexity (GeeksforGeeks, Baeldung, and the cited Sedgewick & Wayne sections), essentially all of them describe auxiliary space and in-place-ness in purely asymptotic terms with a handful of asserted byte figures at most; none attempt to measure a stack frame's real size, and I could not find a comparable published walkthrough of the stack-size-differencing technique this article uses and that I independently validated. I found no factual error in any claim, quote, citation, or piece of arithmetic in this article.

issues.location: 'In place doesn't mean free', paragraph after the quicksort-depth output: 'a sorted array of about 20,000 items -- four times the size just sorted above -- would be well on its way to the ~14,300-frame ceiling the previous section measured on a 1 MiB stack'
issues.problem: A sorted array of n items drives QuickSortInPlace to depth n-1, so 20,000 items means depth 19,999 -- already above the ~14,300-frame ceiling the article itself just cited for plain RecursiveSum frames, before even accounting for the same sentence's admission that quicksort's frames are a little larger than RecursiveSum's. 'Well on its way to' undersells this: by the article's own numbers a 20,000-item sorted array recursing on a 1 MiB stack would already have crossed that ceiling, not merely be approaching it.
issues.fixLooksLike: Say 'would already be past the ~14,300-frame ceiling' or pick a smaller example (e.g. 10,000 items, depth 9,999) if the intent is genuinely to show a case that is close to, but under, the limit.
